articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers

takeaways: Faculty development programs that address resistance and build confidence are critical for embedding AI literacy in curricula — prioritise change management alongside technical training.
Public health educators need structured support to move from AI scepticism to practical readiness; consider peer learning, hands-on workshops, and clear use cases relevant to the discipline.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context and digital competencies specific to that region; transferability to Australian healthcare settings would require adaptation for local regulatory, system, and workforce differences.
takeaways: Competency frameworks for digital literacy should be tailored to specific sectors and roles rather than generic; consider developing role-specific AI capabilities profiles for your workforce based on job functions and responsibilities.

European public health competency frameworks emphasise both technical skills and softer competencies (communication, critical thinking, ethical reasoning); ensure your AI upskilling programs address capability gaps beyond technical knowledge.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education contexts and curriculum design frameworks, which may not directly transfer to adult employee development or organisational settings in Australia.
takeaways: AI literacy for general audiences requires integration with broader digital skills (e.g., data interpretation, critical evaluation) rather than taught as a standalone topic — consider how to embed AI concepts within existing capability frameworks in your organisation.

Middle school frameworks emphasise foundational AI understanding (how systems work, limitations, ethical use) — similar pedagogical scaffolding may help adult employees move from zero to functional AI literacy before task-specific training.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client data and surveys, but findings reflect primarily large organisations and may not fully represent SMEs or non-English-speaking regions.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation will be augmented vs. displaced by generative AI, then prioritise upskilling plans accordingly rather than applying a blanket approach.

Design reskilling pathways that combine AI literacy fundamentals with role-specific applications — generic AI training alone won't prepare employees to use these tools effectively in their actual work.

Build a skills inventory now to understand gaps between current capabilities and future AI-enabled roles, allowing you to target investment in high-impact areas rather than reactive hiring or redeployment.

articles.title: We’re all techies now: Digital skill building for the future - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: We’re all techies now: Digital skill building for the future  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client data and surveys, but specific sample composition, size, and sector breakdown are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Design targeted digital skill-building programs that treat technology literacy as a foundational capability for all roles, not just IT-focused positions.
Identify which 'techie' skills are most critical for your organisation's future strategy, then build role-specific pathways rather than one-size-fits-all training.
Create accountability structures where managers actively support their teams' digital upskilling, positioning it as essential to career progression rather than optional professional development.

articles.title: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design - Frontiers
articles.snippet: A workflow-aligned framework for AI literacy in materials-informatics education: scientific judgment, equity, and curriculum design  Frontiers

Prioritise scientific judgment and critical evaluation of AI outputs as core literacy outcomes, not just technical skills or tool proficiency.
Consider equity explicitly in curriculum design — ensure AI literacy programmes don't widen gaps between students with different prior exposure to AI tools and concepts.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — likely limited by sector, organization type, or geographic scope not evident from title. Full paper review needed to assess applicability to Australian organizational contexts.
takeaways: AI adoption in organizations can paradoxically suppress creativity alongside enhancing it — design implementation strategies that explicitly protect space for novel thinking and experimentation, not just task efficiency.

Monitor employee perceptions and psychological responses during AI rollout; the 'double-edged' effect suggests some staff may experience autonomy loss or skill devaluation, requiring targeted change management and reskilling support.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — article type and geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone; generalisability depends on sample size, industry sectors studied, and country of origin, which are not indicated.
takeaways: Transformational leadership can buffer employees' job insecurity when AI is being implemented — leaders who inspire and support employees during technological change help mitigate anxiety about role displacement.

Building self-efficacy around AI use is protective — employees who feel confident in their ability to work with or adapt to AI tools experience lower job insecurity, suggesting targeted upskilling and confidence-building interventions are worth prioritising.

AI implementation alone does not guarantee job insecurity — the outcome depends critically on organisational leadership quality and employee capability development, giving you concrete levers to manage the psychological impact of technological change.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The mechanism proposed (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) may vary significantly by organisational culture, industry, and leadership quality, limiting broad application.
takeaways: Leaders adopting AI must actively protect psychological safety — create explicit forums for employees to voice concerns about AI implementation without fear of consequences, as reduced safety appears to mediate negative mental health outcomes.

Ethical leadership during AI transitions is protective: demonstrate transparent decision-making about AI use, acknowledge legitimate employee anxieties about automation and job security, and involve staff in governance decisions to buffer against depression and disengagement.

Screen for depression and wellbeing risk during AI rollouts, especially among employees with lower baseline psychological safety, rather than assuming adoption is universally positive for workforce mental health.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet — geographic scope, sector, and sample size unknown. The approach-avoidance framework may apply broadly to AI adoption contexts, but context-specific factors (industry, AI type, organisational culture) likely moderate effects.
takeaways: Employees respond to AI adoption through two distinct behavioural pathways — some actively redesign their work to leverage AI (approach), while others withdraw or resist (avoidance). Managers should identify which employees are in each group and tailor support accordingly.

Job crafting (how employees shape their own roles) is a measurable outcome of AI adoption experiences. Monitor changes in how employees frame and engage with their tasks during AI rollout as an early indicator of adoption success or friction.
Help employees reframe AI as a tool they can shape and control (approach mindset) rather than an external threat — this may encourage proactive job redesign rather than defensive withdrawal.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused perspective on worker uncertainty; findings and policy references may not directly transfer to Australian employment context, which has different legislative frameworks, workplace protections, and industrial relations systems.
takeaways: Identify specific sources of AI-related uncertainty affecting your team (job security, skill relevance, role clarity) and address them directly through transparent communication and upskilling pathways rather than assuming all uncertainty stems from the same cause.

Create psychological safety by acknowledging that uncertainty about AI's impact is normal and widespread, then establish regular feedback mechanisms where employees can voice concerns and co-create solutions with leadership.

Design transition support now (career counselling, skills training, team restructuring plans) for roles most exposed to AI disruption, rather than waiting for uncertainty to escalate into disengagement or turnover.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess from title and snippet alone — full methodology required to determine sample size, geographic scope, and sector representation.
takeaways: Self-efficacy with AI tools appears to be a protective factor for mental health during AI adoption — consider assessing and building confidence in AI capabilities before rolling out new systems to reduce anxiety and stress.

Mental health outcomes during AI implementation may depend less on the technology itself and more on employees' perceived ability to use it effectively — targeted training and support interventions should prioritise confidence-building, not just technical skill transfer.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are drawn from consulting experience but lack specific sample size, sector detail, or geographic scope; findings are likely most applicable to large organisations with resources for structured change programmes.
takeaways: Shift from 'adoption' framing (passive compliance) to 'adaptation' framing (active behaviour change) — this reorientation helps employees see AI integration as a skill-building opportunity rather than a threat, potentially reducing resistance.

Structure change interventions around building specific human behaviours (e.g. prompt engineering, cross-functional collaboration) rather than simply rolling out AI tools; this targeted approach increases the likelihood that employees develop genuine capability rather than surface-level familiarity.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — would depend on study sample size, sectors included, and geographic scope. Frontiers publishes globally, but specific sampling details are not provided.
takeaways: Employees respond to AI adoption through two competing psychological pathways: approach (seeking opportunities to upskill and redefine roles) and avoidance (withdrawing or resisting change) — understanding which dominates in your team helps you design targeted support interventions.

Job crafting (how employees reshape their tasks and roles) is a key mechanism linking AI adoption to engagement outcomes — proactively facilitating role redefinition conversations during AI rollout can shift employee responses from defensive to adaptive.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on global consulting experience, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic focus are unclear from the snippet provided. takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge requiring systematic reskilling and role redesign, not just technology implementation — this shifts focus from tools to people and culture change.
Design change initiatives that address both technical AI literacy and behavioural readiness (e.g., managing uncertainty, adapting to new workflows) to improve adoption rates and reduce resistance.
Establish clear role pathways and career narratives for employees transitioning into or alongside AI-enabled work to maintain engagement and reduce attrition during transformation.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — Stanford GSB perspectives on AI and work trends may reflect US higher education and elite business contexts; applicability to broader Australian organisational contexts unclear without detail on sample or methodology.
takeaways: Identify which specific work processes in your organisation are most susceptible to AI disruption, then design upskilling interventions targeted at those areas rather than generic AI literacy.
Establish clear communication channels to address employee concerns about job displacement early—research shows proactive transparency about AI implementation reduces resistance and anxiety.

Map the specific competencies (e.g., complex judgment, stakeholder management) that AI cannot replace in your roles, and emphasise these in role design and performance conversations to build employee confidence.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across clients, but specific case examples and implementation details may reflect large enterprises primarily.
takeaways: Map AI transformation in stages (adoption, scaling, impact) rather than treating it as a single change initiative — this helps teams maintain momentum and reset expectations as each horizon requires different skills, governance, and organisational readiness.

Identify early wins in the first horizon to build internal credibility and stakeholder buy-in, which is essential before attempting organisation-wide or cross-functional AI adoption in later horizons.

Allocate change resources and capability-building programmes differently across the three horizons — early adoption needs different support (experimentation, risk tolerance) than scaling or embedding impact (process change, measurement, compliance).

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone; full article review needed to determine sample size, geographic scope, sector focus, and methodology.
takeaways: Self-efficacy is a key psychological factor influencing how employees experience mental health outcomes during AI adoption — focus upskilling and training programmes on building confidence and competence with AI tools, not just technical skills.

Mental health impacts during technological change are significant enough to warrant proactive support; screen for anxiety or stress during AI implementation and pair technical transition with psychological support or wellbeing resources.

Design AI adoption rollouts to scaffold self-efficacy early — start with lower-stakes, high-success tasks to build confidence before moving to complex applications, reducing mental health strain and improving engagement.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident in the title and snippet; geographic scope and participant demographics are unclear.
takeaways: People don't all remember surprising moments the same way — your personality shapes what sticks in your mind from unexpected events.
This suggests why eyewitness accounts of the same surprising incident can differ dramatically between people, even when they witnessed it together.
It's a counterintuitive reminder that memory isn't a neutral recording device; our individual traits actively filter and encode what we find memorable.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Broad — draws on established psychological research on social connection and health outcomes, though specific studies cited may vary in geographic scope.
takeaways: Strong friendships appear to have measurable health benefits comparable to other major lifestyle factors — a surprisingly underrated lever for wellbeing that most people instinctively know but rarely prioritise.
The mechanism isn't just emotional comfort; social connection influences immune function, stress hormones, and even longevity — showing that 'it's all in your head' is literally backwards.
Quality matters more than quantity — a few close friendships deliver more health bang for buck than a large shallow network, which runs counter to social media's emphasis on follower counts.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Limited — article appears to be a news summary of research findings without details on the original study's sample, methodology, or geographic scope.
takeaways: Emerging research suggests genetics play a larger role in personality formation than previously thought, challenging the long-standing nature-vs-nurture debate.
This finding is counterintuitive because it goes against decades of psychological emphasis on environmental and experiential factors shaping who we are.
It's a reminder that personality isn't simply malleable through willpower or therapy alone — there's a biological blueprint we all inherit that influences our temperament and behaviour.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest universal patterns in how personality traits relate to music preferences across diverse cultural contexts.
takeaways: People with similar personality types gravitate toward the same genres worldwide, suggesting music taste is a personality fingerprint that transcends culture and geography.
The link between personality and music is so consistent globally that your Spotify playlist might reveal more about your temperament than any questionnaire could.
This challenges the idea that musical taste is purely culturally determined — there's a universal human logic to what kinds of music appeal to different personality types.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone; typical of psychology literature reviews covering theoretical frameworks rather than empirical findings from specific populations.
takeaways: True crime obsession isn't morbid curiosity — psychologists have identified genuine cognitive reasons (pattern-recognition, safety learning, narrative closure-seeking) that explain why millions find murder mysteries compelling.

The appeal cuts across demographics in surprising ways: it's not just thrill-seekers or detectives-in-training, but ordinary people satisfying deep psychological needs through vicarious problem-solving.

Understanding the psychology behind true crime fandom reveals how humans use storytelling to process danger and uncertainty — the same mental machinery that helped our ancestors survive now keeps us binge-watching documentaries.

topics.label: Psychological Safety

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on the specific sample composition, geography, and industry sectors studied. The causal pathways between AI adoption, psychological safety, ethical leadership, and depression require validation across different organisational contexts and cultures.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health when organisations fail to maintain psychological safety and ethical leadership practices — prioritise transparent communication about AI implementation and actively solicit employee concerns to maintain trust.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions: leaders must visibly model ethical decision-making around AI use, clarify how AI affects roles and job security, and ensure employees feel safe raising concerns without fear of repercussions.

Monitor psychological safety as a key indicator during AI rollouts — conduct pulse surveys or focus groups to detect whether employees feel secure sharing doubts about AI systems, and address gaps before they compound into depression and disengagement.

articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC

takeaways: Identify which psychological safety concerns (e.g., fear of job displacement, worry about skill relevance, anxiety about organisational change) are most prevalent in your workforce to prioritise targeted interventions.

Use global benchmark data on employee hopes and fears to assess how your organisation's psychological safety climate compares, revealing gaps between what employees worry about and what leadership assumes they care about.
Design communications and safety-building initiatives that directly address the top fears identified in the survey to build trust and demonstrate that leadership understands employee concerns.

articles.snippet: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems  Frontiers

Psychological safety in high-acuity clinical settings requires attention to how performance expectations interact with individual wellbeing — consider how your organisation communicates these connections to staff.

articles.title: Fostering Ethical Conduct Through Psychological Safety - MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.snippet: Fostering Ethical Conduct Through Psychological Safety  MIT Sloan Management Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — draws on research and practitioner insights but lacks primary empirical data; insights are likely applicable across sectors and geographies, though specific organisational contexts may vary.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that separate the person from the behaviour when discussing ethical lapses — this reduces defensive reactions and encourages honest reflection on misconduct without threatening psychological safety.

Use structured conversations (e.g., pre-mortems, ethics simulations) where employees can discuss ethical dilemmas in low-stakes settings before real situations arise, building confidence to raise concerns.

Ensure leaders visibly acknowledge and learn from their own ethical missteps without defensiveness — this models vulnerability and signals that the organisation values integrity over reputation-protection.
